raw_case_text:
A 71-year-old man, with a past medical history significant for acute myeloid leukemia, underwent induction with cytarabine and idarubicin followed by consolidation with three cycles of high-dose cytarabine. After one year of achieving remission, he was found to have relapsed leukemia during workup for anemia. He was admitted to the hospital for salvage chemotherapy with cytarabine and mitoxantrone. Ten days after salvage chemotherapy, he developed a neutropenic fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and elevated total bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound showed no signs of biliary obstruction. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed pericecal inflammatory stranding without pneumatosis concerning cecal typhlitis as well as an "apple-core mass" of the ascending colon near the hepatic flexure concerning colon cancer (Figure 1).
Colonoscopy was deferred because he was critically ill with neutropenic enterocolitis. Despite initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics consisting of vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, his clinical condition deteriorated. He was transferred to the medical intensive care unit with acute respiratory failure requiring assisted ventilation for several days. Blood cultures revealed Granulicatella adjacens and transthoracic echocardiogram revealed an aortic valve vegetation consistent with endocarditis requiring 6 weeks treatment with intravenous vancomycin. Additionally, he was noted to have hyperbilirubinemia secondary to hepatic veno-occlusive disease for which he completed a course of defibrotide with eventual normalization of liver enzymes. The patient improved clinically, and subsequent bone marrow biopsy obtained 7 weeks after induction chemotherapy showed no evidence of leukemia. After six weeks of inpatient treatment and subsequent clinical improvement, a colonoscopy was performed to rule out colon cancer given the suspicious apple-core lesion noted on the CT at the hepatic flexure. It revealed diffuse friable changes of the colonic wall extending from the cecum to the hepatic flexure and the transverse colon (Figure 2). Biopsies of the ascending colon, cecum, hepatic flexure, and transverse colon were taken. He was discharged to acute rehabilitation due to deconditioning and a 55 pound weight loss after 7 weeks of inpatient hospitalization.
Final pathology from the cecal biopsy specimens showed chronic active colitis with cryptitis, ulceration, and architectural distortion (Figure 3). CMV immunohistochemical staining was positive for CMV type inclusions compatible with CMV colitis (Figure 4). The biopsies were negative for dysplasia and malignancy. The ascending colon, hepatic flexure mass, and transverse colon mass were negative for CMV inclusions on immunohistochemical stains but showed features consistent with chronic active colitis with cryptitis and architectural distortion.
Our patient remained asymptomatic, without recurrence of diarrhea, fever, or abdominal pain.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old man with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia developed neutropenic fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and hyperbilirubinemia 10 days after salvage cytarabine and mitoxantrone chemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having relapsed 1 year after initial AML remission (previously treated with cytarabine + idarubicin induction and 3 cycles of high-dose cytarabine consolidation), the patient received inpatient salvage chemotherapy with cytarabine and mitoxantrone. Ten days post-chemotherapy, he developed febrile neutropenia, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and hyperbilirubinemia, and subsequently deteriorated on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam with acute respiratory failure requiring ICU transfer and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) status post prior cytarabine/idarubicin induction, 3 cycles of high-dose cytarabine consolidation, and current salvage cytarabine/mitoxantrone chemotherapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for neutropenic fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, jaundice/hyperbilirubinemia, acute respiratory failure, and a 55-pound hospital weight loss with deconditioning.

objective.physical_examination: Critically ill with neutropenic enterocolitis and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, followed by severe deconditioning and a 55-pound weight loss over a 7-week hospitalization.
objective.routine_investigations: Elevated total bilirubin and liver enzymes (secondary to hepatic veno-occlusive disease, normalized after defibrotide). Blood cultures grew Granulicatella adjacens. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary obstruction; transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed an aortic valve vegetation consistent with infective endocarditis.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominopelvic CT on day 10 post-chemotherapy demonstrated pericecal inflammatory fat stranding without pneumatosis (concerning for cecal typhlitis) and an 'apple-core' mass in the ascending colon near the hepatic flexure concerning for colon carcinoma. Bone marrow biopsy at week 7 confirmed complete leukemia remission. Colonoscopy performed after 6 weeks of inpatient recovery revealed diffuse friable colonic mucosa extending from the cecum to the hepatic flexure and transverse colon; histopathological examination of the cecal biopsy demonstrated chronic active colitis with cryptitis, ulceration, architectural distortion, and positive CMV immunohistochemical staining for CMV inclusion bodies (while biopsies of the ascending colon, hepatic flexure mass, and transverse colon showed chronic active colitis negative for malignancy, dysplasia, and CMV inclusions).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cecal cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis presenting as neutropenic typhlitis and an ascending colon inflammatory pseudotumor ('apple-core' lesion mimicking colon adenocarcinoma) following salvage AML chemotherapy, confirmed by positive CMV immunohistochemical staining and chronic active ulcerative colitis on cecal biopsy (with colonic malignancy ruled out), complicated by Granulicatella adjacens aortic valve endocarditis and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD). Treated with a 6-week course of intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, defibrotide for hepatic VOD, and ICU supportive care, achieving complete AML bone marrow remission and resolution of diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain without antiviral therapy requirement at rehabilitation discharge.
